extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, practitioners, and general readers interested in narrative (literary) journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for producing and understanding narrative (literary) journalism—long-form news writing that applies literary devices and storytelling structures to reportage. Covers characteristics, structure, voice, formats, and multimedia adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: literary devices applied to news
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative journalism, or literary journalism, is a form of creative nonfiction in which the author applies the literary devices and stylistic features of fiction to a news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames the genre: reporters borrow fiction techniques (style, devices) while reporting factual events; the piece remains journalism rather than pure fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three structural aspects: setting, complication, outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative journalism is composed of three aspects: setting (the context behind the story), complication (the main events of the story) and outcome (the story's aftermath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should establish context, present the central events/conflicts, and show consequences or aftermath—mirroring story arcs from fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative structure: chronological order or episodes (not inverted pyramid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas regular news reports follow the inverted pyramid format, narrative journalists generally present their pieces in chronological order or divide them into episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer chronological progression or episodic organization to build narrative momentum and comprehension rather than front-loading facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of literary devices (suspense, flashbacks, flashforwards)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative journalist may employ literary devices like suspense, flashbacks and flashforwards to engage his audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques that manipulate time or tension can be used to increase engagement; apply carefully to maintain factual clarity and avoid misleading chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray events as plot and people as characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece may be written as if the events covered were parts of a plot and the people involved were characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scene-setting, dialogue, and character-focused details to dramatize real events while preserving accuracy and avoiding fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person narration / author as character
rubrics_metrics.description: Many narrative journalists write in first-person, thereby including themselves as characters, to create the appearance of a connection between themselves and their stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person can provide intimacy and perspective; consider transparency about the reporter's role and maintain ethical boundaries between participation and observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible presence of a moral
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a moral in a work of narrative journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative pieces can convey social values or lessons, but reporters should distinguish moral/interpretive elements from factual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater coverage of context and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative journalism gives more coverage than regular news reporting does to the contexts of and circumstances behind events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide background, environment, historical and social context to help readers understand why events occurred, not just what happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate sources' thoughts to explain motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative journalists attempt to make their readers understand their sources' motives and actions by incorporating their sources' thoughts into their pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of sources' perspectives and interiority should be based on reporting (quotes, observed behavior, documented statements) and clearly attributed to avoid imaginings presented as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulate literary fiction's prose style
rubrics_metrics.description: Written narrative journalism emulates literary fiction's style of prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt richer, craft-focused prose: careful word selection, concrete description, scene construction and literary rhythm—while ensuring factual fidelity and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to audio media using voice and sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative journalism can be created in other media, such as podcasts and radio broadcasts whose hosts use similar storytelling techniques to written narrative journalism; podcasting and radio permit narrative journalists to make use of sound effects, and their own voices, to express emotions and ideas that cannot be conveyed as strongly in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting to audio, use voice, pacing, sound design and ambient audio to convey atmosphere and emotion responsibly, and retain factual sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multimedia (data visualisations, VR, games, animations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have also used data visualisations, virtual reality, video games and animations to present news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage multimedia to enhance immersion or explanation, but ensure interactive/visual elements accurately represent data and do not mislead the audience about facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete storylines with causal incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative journalism generally contains 'complete' storylines with beginnings, middles and ends, and includes incidents that cause major events later on in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure should show cause-and-effect and narrative causality—include earlier incidents that logically lead to later developments for coherence and explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity and authorial voice vs pure objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers in movements like New Journalism and Gonzo centered their authors' thoughts and experiences, questioning the importance of complete objectivity in journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative forms may foreground subjectivity and interpretation; maintain transparency about subjective choices and preserve standards of verification and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate formats: books, magazines, essays, newspaper long-form
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative journalism has historically appeared in literary form through books, magazines, essays and newspaper articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best suited to longer-form outlets (magazines, books, long online features) that allow sustained narrative development and contextual depth.
